newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi prepares to fly bodies of crash victims home.
newsitem.headline: Saudi prepares to fly bodies of crash victims home.

text.p: Saudi Arabian officials were completing arrangements on Thursday to fly home the bodies of 13 Saudis killed over India in the world's worst mid-air collision in which 349 people died.

"We are in touch with our people in India to finalise the arrangements. We are hoping the bodies might be flown back to Jeddah on Thursday or Friday," one official at the Saudi Arabian Airlines Corp SAUD.CN headquarters in Jeddah said.
"Most of the Saudi bodies have been identified," another official said, but did not say how many.
Saudi newspapers reported on Thursday that 11 Saudi bodies had been identified. The Saudi victims are one passenger and 12 crew members, including five anti-terrorism security men.

The officials said they received on Thursday the final list of passengers and crew on the Boeing 747 when it and an incoming Kazakh plane collided minutes after the Saudi plane took off from New Delhi on Tuesday.

They said they included 230 Indians, 51 Nepalis, 13 Saudis, three Pakistanis, three Americans, three Tunisians and a Briton. Other victims came from Bangladesh, the Philippines, Morocco, Algeria and Jordan.

Indian authorities said they had identified only 131 of 294 bodies found amid the wreckage near New Delhi. A total of 349 passengers and crew, 312 on the Saudi Boeing 747 jet and 37 on the Ilyushin Il-76 freighter, were killed.
Saudi airlines director-general Khaled Ben-Bakr was to hold a news conference at the airline's headquarters at 1000 GMT to give details on the crash, the Saudi officials said.
Saudi Arabia has sent a team to New Delhi to help investigate.
The official said the Saudi airline was in constant touch with the families of the victims and keeping them updated on the expected arrival of the bodies in Jeddah.

The Arab News newspaper said the body of the pilot, Khalid al-Shubaily, 45, had been identified by his brother who flew to New Delhi. It quoted the family as saying they planned to bury him in the Moslem holy city of Medina in Saudi Arabia.

It quoted the Indian ambassador in Riyadh, Mohammad Hamid Ansari, as saying the embassy was gathering information on the Indian victims in an effort to establish if they were entitled to any money from their employers in Saudi Arabia.
"We don't know yet how many were working in the kingdom and how many were visiting," he said.

Oil-rich Saudi Arabia employs an army of foreign workers, many of them from the Indian subcontinent. Most of the crash victims were believed to be returning to their jobs or heading to the kingdom for new jobs.

Aviation experts said the cause of the crash could be known in the next two weeks. Indian officials denied that faulty equipment on the ground or misunderstood instructions from the control tower were to blame.

Saudi Defence and Aviation Minister Prince Sultan suggested on Wednesday that a technical problem or language confusion between the Kazakh pilot and New Delhi's control tower may have caused the collision.
He said the accident was an "act of fate", adding that "nobody had a hand in it" and "there was no foul play".
Asked whether Saudi Arabia would compensate the families of the victims, he replied: "This is always the policy of King Fahd." He did not elaborate.
